name: End School Corporal Punishment — share library
rules: Every number comes from facts/claims with its year; the claim id is on each post.
No students: no photographs or renderings of children being struck.
No contempt for the South, faith, rural life, teachers, or parents who were paddled themselves.
One idea per post: a number, a line, a place to go.

posts.text: If your school still paddles, you can say no — in writing, and the office has to keep it on file. The letter takes two minutes. Every district that stopped, stopped because the pile of refusals got tall. Which districts still do it, and the letter: earthpilot.org/kids

claims.claim: Three states now require a parent's affirmative consent before a school may paddle a child: Missouri (written permission, 2022), Louisiana (annual written consent on a state form, 2023) and Florida (consent for the year or per instance, 2025); Kentucky reached the same rule by regulation in 2022 and every district then quit.

All 115 North Carolina school districts had prohibited corporal punishment by October 2, 2018, when Graham County became the last to vote to end it, although state law (G.S. 115C-390.4) still permits it.

posts.text: 33 states stopped paddling students. Their schools are fine. Kentucky's last district stopped in 2023 and the state recorded zero instances the next year. See whether your district still does it: earthpilot.org/kids

claims.claim: Kentucky recorded zero instances of corporal punishment in the 2023-24 school year after all 171 school districts adopted prohibiting policies by November 2, 2023, driven by a state board regulation rather than a statute.

As of September 2026, corporal punishment in public schools is legal by statute in 17 states; in two of them, Kentucky and North Carolina, every district has prohibited it by policy, leaving 15 where it is both legal and in use.

posts.text: Nobody takes the paddle away and puts nothing in its place — that's how you get a suspension spike and a board that reverses itself. Ten free training modules, written for small schools with no behavior specialist: classroom routines, the office ladder, the five-minute repair. earthpilot.org/kids/kit/

claims.claim: In a five-year randomized trial across 37 Maryland elementary schools, School-Wide Positive Behavioral Interventions and Supports reduced suspensions and office referrals, and children in PBIS schools were 33 percent less likely to receive an office discipline referral.

posts.text: 19,851 kids were paddled in US public schools in 2023-24, by the government's own count, which it calls likely underreported. Every district that still does it, on one map: earthpilot.org/kids

claims.claim: In the 2023-24 school year, 19,851 K-12 public school students received corporal punishment, computed by this project from the raw Civil Rights Data Collection file released August 31, 2026; the Office for Civil Rights has published no analysis of that release.

The federal count of corporal punishment is self-reported by districts and, in the Department of Education's own words, 'likely underreported'; it counts students, not incidents, and skips virtual schools.

posts.text: 36 of 38 OECD countries ban hitting kids in school. The two that don't: the United States and one Australian state. 137 of 199 countries have ended it. We're late. earthpilot.org/kids

claims.claim: Of the 38 OECD countries, corporal punishment in schools is fully prohibited in 36; the exceptions are the United States and Australia, where Queensland has no statutory ban for non-government schools.
Corporal punishment is fully prohibited in schools in 137 of the 199 states and territories tracked by the Global Initiative to End All Corporal Punishment of Children; in 62 it is not.

posts.text: For any board considering the change: a model policy, the motion, what to say to staff, families and students, and the ninety-day plan — free, as an in-kind grant. The American Academy of Pediatrics asked every state to end the practice in 2023. earthpilot.org/kids/kit/

claims.claim: In August 2023 the American Academy of Pediatrics published a policy statement recommending that corporal punishment in all school settings be abolished in all states by law and replaced by alternative forms of behavior management.

On March 24, 2023, US Secretary of Education Miguel Cardona wrote to every governor and chief state school officer asking states to end corporal punishment in schools, citing federal data that Black students were 2.3 times as likely as white students to receive it and Black girls four times as likely as white girls.

posts.text: Every US school district's corporal punishment policy, read from the district's own documents, sourced and quotable — 1,600 and counting, built by people pointing their AI assistants at one public problem. Look up yours, or bring your agent: earthpilot.org/kids

posts.text: Live in Arkansas, Tennessee, Alabama, Virginia or Delaware? Your state answers public-records requests only from its own residents. Forty-three Arkansas districts are missing from the corporal-punishment record because of it. Lend your standing — thirty seconds, you're copied on everything: earthpilot.org/foia/
